short: Lip-reader text at use time (M07) was ahead and still leads LRS3 WER, but the words come from the lip reader: 19.1% reading WER becomes 21.4%; without it 86.2%.
position: LipVoicer [@yemini2024lipvoicer] changes three components: lip-reader text steers synthesis at use time (M07), a CTC recognizer trained on noised mel-spectrograms carries all text supervision (M02), and a video-conditioned diffusion model generates the mel-spectrogram (M06). The M07 change was ahead at publication: no earlier study among 165 video-to-speech papers uses lip-reader text at inference (pattern match, Appendix), the closest design [@hegde2023towards] is [concurrent], and [later] AUTO-AVSR re-scores still rank it lowest in LRS3 WER [@liang2026sldl2s]. The words come from the lip reader, not the synthesizer: on LRS3 output WER is 21.4% against the lip reader's 19.1%, 5.4% with ground-truth text, and 86.2% without guidance, worse than the Lip2Speech baseline at 57.4% (Tables 4, 6, 7). No baseline received that text, so "state-of-the-art results" (Sec. 1) pit a 2023 lip reader against text-free synthesizers. M02, M06 and M12 are standard; words are scored only by an ASR from the same work as the lip reader.
